notes.content:
Focus: Daily Routines & Intentions

Today's Base Paragraph

"My name is ____. I wake up early every day. I study English for thirty minutes because I want to speak confidently."

1. Vocabulary Breakdown (Verb Forms)

Verbs change depending on when the action happens. Here are the verbs from your paragraph:

Base Form (V1) Past Simple (V2) Past Participle (V3) Continuous (-ing) Meaning / Note
Wake Woke Woken Waking To stop sleeping. (Usually used as "wake up")
Study Studied Studied Studying To learn a subject.
Want Wanted Wanted Wanting To desire something.
Speak Spoke Spoken Speaking To talk / express ideas.

2. Grammar Focus: The Pronoun "I"

Rule 1: Always Capitalized
No matter where "I" is in a sentence (beginning, middle, or end), it must always be a capital letter. Never write it as a lowercase "i".

Rule 2: When & Why to Use It
Use "I" when you are the person performing the action (the subject).
  • Example: I study English. (Correct)
  • Example: Me study English. (Incorrect - "me" is used when the action happens to you).

3. Tense Analysis: Present Simple

Paragraph uses the Present Simple Tense (Subject + V1).

Why did you use it here? Because you are talking about habits, routines, and permanent facts ("every day").

Pro-Tip for Speaking: If the subject is He, She, or It, you must add an -s or -es to the verb!
  • I wake up early. -> He wakes up early.
  • I study English. -> She studies English.

4. Sentence Expansion (Create New Sentences)

Try using your exact sentence structure to talk about different habits:

  • "I go to the gym every day because I want to stay healthy."
  • "I read books for thirty minutes because I want to learn new things."

5. Today's Quiz & Tasks

Task 1: Change the Subject
Rewrite your paragraph as if you are talking about your friend, Sarah. (Remember the -s rule!)

Task 2: Multiple Choice
Which sentence is grammatically correct?




Task 1 Answer: "Her name is Sarah. She wakes up early every day. She studies English for thirty minutes because she wants to speak confidently."

Task 2 Answer: c (a is wrong because "yesterday" needs past tense "woke"; b is wrong because "he" needs "studies").
notes.title: Day - 1

notes.content:
Focus: Speaking Naturally About Your Day

"Every morning, I wake up at 6 o'clock because I want to improve myself. First, I drink a glass of water and then I go for a short walk. Although I sometimes feel tired, I never skip my routine because I know small habits lead to big success. After I come home, I study English for thirty minutes before I start my work. Learning every day makes me more confident, and I believe consistency is more important than perfection."

1. The Big Picture (What it means)

This paragraph is about a simple morning routine built to help you grow. The speaker does a few things in a specific order: gets up early, drinks water, goes for a walk, and studies English before starting their job. Even when they are tired, they keep going because they believe that doing something regularly matters more than doing it perfectly.

2. Verb Forms Discovery (Action Shifters)

Verbs are the engine of your speech. To change when an action happened (past, present, or continuous), you must know how the verb changes shape. Here are the core verbs pulled directly from your paragraph:

Base Form (V1)
Present / Routine		 Past Simple (V2)
Yesterday / Completed		 Past Participle (V3)
Perfect / Completed Life Experience		 Continuous (-ing)
Action Happening Now		 Speaking Tip
Wake (up) Woke (up) Woken (up) Waking (up) Say "I woke up late yesterday" to talk about the past.
Want Wanted Wanted Wanting Native speakers rarely say "I am wanting." Stick to "I want."
Improve Improved Improved Improving Add a clean 'd' sound at the end for past tense: /ɪmˈpruːvd/.
Drink Drank Drunk Drinking Make sure to shift the vowel clear from 'i' to 'a' for the past form.
Go Went Gone Going "Went" is completely irregular. Practice saying "I went for a walk."
Feel Felt Felt Feeling Shorten the vowel sound when moving from "feel" to "felt."
Skip Skipped Skipped Skipping Double the letter 'p' when writing the past or continuous forms.
Know Knew Known Knowing The letter 'K' is completely silent in all of these forms.
Lead Led Led Leading Pronounced exactly like the past form of the word "read" (Red).
Come Came Come Coming Notice that the V1 and V3 forms are spelled exactly the same way.
Study Studied Studied Studying Change the 'y' to 'ied' for past forms.
Start Started Started Starting Pronounce the past ending with an extra clear syllable: /id/.
Make Made Made Making A vital high-frequency verb for daily work updates.
Believe Believed Believed Believing Gently bite your lower lip on the 'v' sound at the end.

3. Real-Life Vocabulary (Words you will actually use)

Word & Type How to Say It & Meaning Words that go together (Collocations) Natural Examples for Speaking
Consistency
Noun		 /kənˈsɪs.tən.si/

Doing the same thing regularly to get results.		 Great consistency, lack of consistency. 1. Consistency is the secret to learning a language.
2. Your speaking improves with consistency.
3. I struggle with consistency when I am busy.
Routine
Noun		 /ruːˈtiːn/

Your usual fix of daily habits.		 Morning routine, daily routine, stick to a routine. 1. I need to fix my morning routine.
2. Going to the gym is part of my routine.
3. Don't break your routine on weekends.
Improve
Verb		 /ɪmˈpruːv/

To make something better than it was before.		 Want to improve, drastically improve. 1. I really want to improve my speaking skills.
2. You can improve by practicing every day.
3. The weather is starting to improve.

4. Grammar Discovery: Turning Actions into Names (-ing Words)

Look at this part of your paragraph: "Learning every day makes me more confident..."

  • What is it? We call this a Gerund. It is just a verb with "-ing" added to it, but it acts like a regular noun (a name of a thing).
  • Why is it used here? The speaker wants to talk about the *concept* of learning as a single habit that brings a result.
  • When to use it: Use it whenever you want to start a sentence with an activity as the main topic. (e.g., Cooking is fun, Running is hard).
  • When NOT to use it: Do not use it if you are talking about an action you are doing right now. (Say "I am learning right now," NOT "Learning right now").
  • Formula: Action-ing + Verb with 's' + Object
Common Mistake:
❌ Speak English daily makes me confident.
✅ Speaking English daily makes me confident. (Always add -ing when the action is the subject, and add 's' to the next verb!).

5 Natural Examples to Use While Speaking:

  1. Waking up early gives me more free time.
  2. Practicing daily helps me talk faster.
  3. Reading books expands my vocabulary.
  4. Drinking water keeps me energized.
  5. Skipping meals makes me feel tired.

5. The Tiny Words (Fluency Boosters)

  • at (at 6 o'clock): Used because it marks an exact spot on the clock.
  • for (for thirty minutes): Used to show how long an action lasted (a block of time).
  • although (Although I feel tired): Used to connect a problem with an action that happened anyway. (Note: Never use "but" in the same sentence with although!).
  • because (because I want to): Used to give the direct reason for your action.

6. Sentence Blueprints (Copy and Paste These)

Try using these exact patterns to talk about different areas of your life:

  • Pattern 1: "After I [Action 1], I [Action 2] before I start my work."
    Your new example: "After I drink coffee, I check my schedule before I start my work."
  • Pattern 2: "Although I sometimes feel [Negative Feeling], I never skip [My Habit]."
    Your new example: "Although I sometimes feel lazy, I never skip my gym session."

7. Tense Check: Why Present Simple?

This paragraph uses the Present Simple Tense (I wake up, I drink, I study). We use this because we are talking about permanent habits and routines. We do NOT use the Present Continuous ("I am waking up") because you aren't describing what you are doing at this exact second; you are describing your life style.

8. Speaking & Pronunciation Room

1. Word Stress (Say it loud):
When speaking, put extra energy on the most important words: "Every MORNING, I wake up at SIX o'clock..."

2. Shadowing Exercise:
Read the sentence along with a timer. Try to group words together naturally without stopping: "Although I sometimes feel tired... [pause] ...I never skip my routine."

9. Quick Writing & Correction Labs

Fix the Error: "Every day, swim keeps me healthy and happy."

Correction: "Every day, swimming keeps me healthy and happy." (Needs the -ing form as the subject).

10. Moving Forward (70% Old + 30% New)

In our last lesson, you learned basic sentences like *"I study English."* Today, we took that exact idea and added **Time Markers** (*First, then, after*) and **Obstacles** (*Although I feel tired*). Next time, we will use these same habits to talk about what you *used* to do in the past.

11. Tonight's Homework Challenge

  1. Speaking (5 mins): Look in the mirror and say your paragraph out loud 3 times without looking at the paper.
  2. Writing (10 mins): Use Blueprint 2 to write one sentence about a habit you do even when you are busy or lazy.
  3. Quiz (5 mins): Complete the 3 interactive questions below!

Quick Fluency Check

1. Which sentence sounds natural and correct?

2. Fill the blank: "________ every day helps me speak clearly."

3. Yesterday, I ________ three glasses of water before lunch.
notes.title: Day - 2

notes.content:
Day - 3 • Expressing Daily Habits Step-by-Step

"I wake up at six. I drink a glass of water. I open the window. I breathe the fresh air. I eat a healthy breakfast. I read a book. I study English every day. I write in my notebook. I learn new words. I practice speaking every evening. I enjoy my routine. I sleep at ten."

1. The Big Picture (What it means)

This paragraph walks through a complete, healthy day from start to finish. It outlines a step-by-step habit loop: waking up early at 6 AM, refreshing the body and mind (water, fresh air, healthy breakfast), dedicating focused time to self-improvement (reading, writing, practicing English), and ending the day peacefully with sleep at 10 PM.

2. Verb Forms Discovery (Action Engine)

Here are all 12 action verbs from today's paragraph. Mastering these forms allows you to effortlessly shift your story between what you do every day (V1) and what you did yesterday (V2):

Base Form (V1)
Habit / Everyday		 Past Simple (V2)
Yesterday / Past		 Past Participle (V3)
Completed Action		 Continuous (-ing)
Action Happening Now		 Speaking Tip
Wake Woke Woken Waking Usually paired with "up": "I wake up early."
Drink Drank Drunk Drinking Notice the vowel shift: Drink (present) $\rightarrow$ Drank (past).
Open Opened Opened Opening Soft 'd' sound at the end in past tense: /oʊpənd/.
Breathe Breathed Breathed Breathing Ends with a soft 'th' sound. Don't confuse with the noun "breath."
Eat Ate Eaten Eating Past form "ate" is pronounced like the number "eight."
Read Read Read Reading Spelled the same in past, but pronounced like the color "red"!
Study Studied Studied Studying Drop the 'y' and add 'ied' for the past tense.
Write Wrote Written Writing The 'W' is silent! Pronounce as "rite" and "rote."
Learn Learned / Learnt Learned / Learnt Learning Both "learned" and "learnt" are correct and natural.
Practice Practiced Practiced Practicing Ends with a soft 'st' sound in the past tense: /ˈpræktɪst/.
Enjoy Enjoyed Enjoyed Enjoying Stress the second syllable: en-JOY.
Sleep Slept Slept Sleeping Vowel shortens in the past: Sleep $\rightarrow$ Slept.

3. Real-Life Vocabulary (Useful Daily Words)

Word & Type How to Say It & Meaning Words that go together (Collocations) Natural Examples for Speaking
Healthy
Adjective		 /ˈhel.θi/

Good for your body and mind.		 Healthy breakfast, healthy lifestyle, healthy habit. 1. I try to eat a healthy breakfast every morning.
2. Walking daily is a healthy habit.
3. Staying hydrated keeps you healthy.
Practice
Verb		 /ˈpræk.tɪs/

Doing an activity regularly to become good at it.		 Practice speaking, practice daily, need to practice. 1. I practice speaking English with my friends.
2. You must practice if you want to improve.
3. I practice playing guitar after work.
Routine
Noun		 /ruːˈtiːn/

A fixed set of actions you do regularly.		 Daily routine, enjoy my routine, stick to a routine. 1. I really enjoy my morning routine.
2. Having a routine saves time.
3. My routine changes on weekends.

4. Grammar Discovery: Connecting Actions with "-ing" Words

In our last lesson, we learned how Gerunds act as subjects (e.g., "Learning every day makes me confident"). Today, look at another natural way we use "-ing" after verbs like practice or enjoy!

  • What is it? When one action verb follows words like practice, enjoy, or stop, the second verb MUST take "-ing".
  • Why is it used here? In "I practice speaking," the word "speaking" acts as the thing/activity you are practicing.
  • When to use it: Whenever you describe an activity that you practice, enjoy, finish, or keep doing.
  • When NOT to use it: Don't use "to" between these verbs (Do NOT say "I practice to speak").
  • Formula: Subject + Practice / Enjoy + Verb-ing
Common Mistake:
❌ I practice speak English every evening. / I practice to speak English.
✅ I practice speaking English every evening.

5 Natural Examples for Daily Speaking:

  1. I enjoy reading books in the quiet morning.
  2. She practices writing new sentences every day.
  3. We enjoy walking in the fresh air.
  4. He practices listening to English podcasts.
  5. They enjoy learning new skills together.

5. The Tiny Words (Fluency Boosters)

  • at (at six / at ten): Used to point to a specific, exact time on the clock.
  • a (a glass / a book / a healthy breakfast): Used before single, countable things mentioned generally for the first time.
  • the (the window / the fresh air): Used when talking about something specific that both the speaker and listener know (e.g., the window in your room).
  • in (in my notebook): Used because the writing goes *inside* the pages of the notebook.

6. Sentence Blueprints (Speaking Linkers)

Your short paragraph has 12 quick sentences. Native speakers combine short sentences using simple connection words like and, then, and after to speak smoothly!

  • Blueprint 1 (Combining Actions): "I wake up at six and drink a glass of water."
  • Blueprint 2 (Sequential Flow): "First, I open the window to breathe fresh air. Then, I eat a healthy breakfast."
  • Blueprint 3 (Activity Linker): "I study English by writing in my notebook and practicing speaking every evening."

7. Tense Check: Present Simple vs. Present Continuous

Today's paragraph uses the Present Simple Tense (I wake, I drink, I study) because it describes a regular daily routine.

Why not Present Continuous? If you say "I am drinking water," it means you have a glass in your hand right this second. To tell someone about your life habits, stick to Present Simple ("I drink water every morning").

8. Speaking & Pronunciation Room

1. Pronunciation Tip (Word Linking):
Native speakers connect the end of one word to the beginning of the next word if it starts with a vowel:
  • "wake up" sounds like "wa-kup"
  • "drink a" sounds like "drin-ka"
  • "eat a" sounds like "ee-ta"

2. Dialogue Role-Play (Practice reading both sides out loud):
Friend: "What time do you usually wake up?"
You: "I wake up at six every morning."
Friend: "What is the first thing you do?"
You: "I drink a glass of water and open the window to breathe fresh air."
Friend: "When do you practice English?"
You: "I study in the morning and practice speaking every evening!"

9. Quick Writing & Correction Labs

1. Fix the Error: "I enjoy to read books and practice to speak English."

Correction: "I enjoy reading books and practice speaking English." (After 'enjoy' and 'practice', always use -ing!).

2. Sentence Building: Combine these three short ideas into one smooth sentence: "I study English. I write in my notebook. I learn new words."

Example: "I study English by writing in my notebook to learn new words."

10. Moving Forward (70% Old + 30% New)

70% Old Review: We are reinforcing your morning routine structure and habit-building mindset (*Present Simple*, exact clock times with *at*, time duration with *for*).

30% New Concept: Today, we added verb linking with -ing (*practice speaking*, *enjoy reading*) and combining short choppy sentences into smooth, flowing speech using *and*, *then*, and *by*.

11. Tonight's Homework Challenge

  1. Speaking (5 mins): Stand up and speak your 12-sentence routine out loud, linking "wake up" to "wa-kup" and "drink a" to "drin-ka."
  2. Writing (10 mins): Write 3 original sentences about what you enjoy doing or practicing in the evening using the Verb + -ing pattern.
  3. Quiz (5 mins): Complete the interactive self-test below!

Quick Fluency Check

1. Which sentence is correctly written and natural?

2. What is the correct past simple (V2) form of 'read' in "Yesterday I _____ a book"?

3. Choose the correct preposition: "I sleep _____ ten o'clock."
notes.title: Day - 3

notes.content:
Daily English Fluency Session

Lesson 3 • Master Daily Routines, Tiny Words, and Long Conversations

"I wake up at 6:00 a.m. I take a bath and eat my breakfast before 9:00 a.m. After that, I study for two hours. Then, I take a 20-minute break. After the break, I study again for two hours. At 1:00 p.m., I eat my lunch. After lunch, I sleep for two hours. At 4:00 p.m., I start studying again for two or three hours. At 5:00 p.m., I usually have a cup of tea. After finishing my tea, I go to the gym. Before 9:00 p.m., I eat my dinner. Then, I go to bed at 11:00 p.m."

1. Verb Forms Discovery (Action Engine)

Every verb changes form based on time. Use V1 for daily habits, V2 for past events, V3 for completed actions, and -ing for actions happening right now.

Base Form (V1)
Habit / Everyday		 Past Simple (V2)
Yesterday / Past		 Past Participle (V3)
Completed Action		 Continuous (-ing)
Happening Now		 Speaking Tip
Wake Woke Woken Waking Paired with "up": "I woke up early yesterday."
Take Took Taken Taking Used for baths, breaks, and time: "I take a break."
Eat Ate Eaten Eating "Ate" sounds like the number eight.
Study Studied Studied Studying Drop the 'y' and add 'ied' for the past tense.
Sleep Slept Slept Sleeping Vowel shortens in the past: Sleep turns to Slept.
Start Started Started Starting Pronounce past ending as an extra syllable: /id/.
Have Had Had Having Used for meals and drinks: "I have tea."
Finish Finished Finished Finishing Ends with a soft 't' sound in past: /fɪnɪʃt/.
Go Went Gone Going "Went" is completely irregular. Practice: "I went to bed."

2. Real-Life Vocabulary

Word & Type How to Say It & Meaning Common Collocations Natural Examples for Speaking
Break
Noun		 /breɪk/

A short pause in work or study.		 Take a break, short break, lunch break. 1. I take a 20-minute break after studying.
2. Let's take a short coffee break.
3. Don't skip your lunch break.
Usually
Adverb		 /ˈjuː.ʒu.ə.li/

Most of the time; as a habit.		 Usually have, usually go, as I usually do. 1. I usually have tea at 5:00 p.m.
2. She usually wakes up early.
3. We usually eat dinner together.
Routine
Noun		 /ruːˈtiːn/

A fixed set of daily habits.		 Daily routine, study routine, stick to a routine. 1. My daily routine helps me stay focused.
2. I try not to break my study routine.
3. Having a routine saves energy.

3. Grammar Discovery: "Have, Has, and Had" Masterclass

In your paragraph, you said: "I usually have a cup of tea." Understanding how to use have, has, and had correctly is one of the biggest leaps in English fluency.

1. HAVE (Present Tense — I, You, We, They)

When to use: Use with I, You, We, They to talk about possessions, meals, drinks, routines, or experiences in the present.

How to use:

  • Meals/Drinks: "I have breakfast at 8:00 a.m." / "We have lunch together."
  • Possession: "I have a study schedule."
  • Actions: "They have a break."

Formula: Subject (I/You/We/They) + HAVE + Object

2. HAS (Present Tense — He, She, It, Single Name)

When to use: Use when the subject is He, She, It, or a person's name (like Rahul or Priya) in the present time.

How to use:

  • Meals/Drinks: "She has a cup of tea at 5:00 p.m."
  • Possession: "He has a busy routine."

Formula: Subject (He/She/It/Name) + HAS + Object

3. HAD (Past Tense — ALL Subjects: I, You, He, She, We, They)

When to use: Use for past actions, meals, or possessions that are completely finished.

How to use:

  • Past Meals/Drinks: "I had dinner at 8:30 p.m. yesterday."
  • Past Routine: "She had a long study session yesterday."

Formula: Subject (ANY) + HAD + Object

Common Mistakes to Avoid:
❌ He have a cup of tea every evening. $\rightarrow$ ✅ He has a cup of tea every evening.
❌ Yesterday I have lunch at 2:00 p.m. $\rightarrow$ ✅ Yesterday I had lunch at 2:00 p.m.
❌ I am having a car. (For possession, do not use -ing) $\rightarrow$ ✅ I have a car.

4. Tiny Words Deep-Dive (Fluency Engine)

Tiny words are the glue of speaking English naturally. Here is the exact guide on how, where, and when to use the tiny words from your paragraph.

1. AT

Where to use: Before exact clock times, specific points in the day, or specific locations.

When to use: When pointing to a precise moment without any duration.

How to use: Place "at" directly before the time or place.

  • "I wake up at 6:00 a.m." (Exact time)
  • "I eat lunch at 1:00 p.m." (Exact time)
  • "I go to bed at 11:00 p.m." (Exact time)
  • "She is at the gym right now." (Exact location)

2. BEFORE

Where to use: Before a specific time, event, or action to show something happens earlier.

When to use: When setting a deadline or indicating priority in time.

How to use: Put "before" right in front of the time phrase or event.

  • "I eat breakfast before 9:00 a.m." (Before a time limit)
  • "I eat dinner before 9:00 p.m." (Before a time limit)
  • "I wash my hands before eating." (Before an action)
  • "Finish your work before you leave." (Before an action)

3. AFTER

Where to use: Before a noun, event, or action to show something happens later.

When to use: To show the next step in a timeline.

How to use: Follow "after" with a noun or a verb taking "-ing".

  • "After that, I study for two hours." (Following an event)
  • "After lunch, I sleep for two hours." (Following a noun)
  • "After finishing my tea, I go to the gym." (Following verb + ing)
  • "After studying, I take a break." (Following verb + ing)

4. FOR

Where to use: Before a duration or span of time.

When to use: When answering "How long does the action last?"

How to use: Pair "for" with numbers and time units (minutes, hours, days).

  • "I study for two hours." (Duration of time)
  • "I take a break for 20 minutes." (Duration of time)
  • "I sleep for two hours." (Duration of time)
  • "I worked for three years at that company." (Duration of time)

5. TO

Where to use: Before a destination or direction.

When to use: When moving from one place toward another place.

How to use: Combine "go/travel/head" + "to" + destination.

  • "I go to the gym." (Direction/Destination)
  • "I go to bed at 11:00 p.m." (Direction/Destination)
  • "She goes to work every morning." (Direction/Destination)
  • "We are travelling to Delhi tomorrow." (Direction/Destination)

5. Sentence Blueprints

Use these exact structural blocks to talk about your day naturally:

  • Blueprint 1 (Deadline Pattern): "I [Action] before [Time/Event]."
    Example: "I complete my assignments before 6:00 p.m."
  • Blueprint 2 (Duration Pattern): "I [Action] for [Number] hours."
    Example: "I exercise at the gym for one hour."
  • Blueprint 3 (Sequential Activity): "After finishing my [Noun/Verb-ing], I [Next Action]."
    Example: "After finishing my work, I spend time with my family."

6. Tense Check: Present Simple vs. Past Simple

This paragraph uses Present Simple because it outlines your daily schedule (routine truth). If you want to talk about what happened yesterday, you must shift every verb into Past Simple (V2):

  • Everyday Routine (Present): "I wake up at 6:00 a.m. and study for two hours."
  • Yesterday's Story (Past): "Yesterday, I woke up at 6:00 a.m. and studied for two hours."

7. Long Conversation Masterclass (How to Keep Talking)

The single biggest issue beginners face is running out of things to say after 2 or 3 short sentences. Here are three simple techniques to build long, natural conversations effortlessly.

Technique 1: The "And-Because-So" Chain Rule

Never end a sentence with just one fact. Attach a reason (using because) or a result (using so).

  • Short/Choppy: "I wake up at 6:00 a.m."
  • Extended Conversation: "I wake up at 6:00 a.m. because I like having quiet time in the morning, so I drink water and study before anyone else gets up."

Technique 2: The "Add a Feeling or Reason" Technique

Whenever you mention an action, follow it up with how you feel about it or why you do it.

  • Fact: "At 5:00 p.m., I usually have a cup of tea."
  • Add Feeling/Reason: "At 5:00 p.m., I usually have a cup of tea. It helps me relax after a long study session, and it gives me energy before heading to the gym."

Technique 3: Long Conversation Role-Play (Practice Out Loud)

Read both sides of this extended conversation to build speaking stamina:

Friend: "Hey, you look super organized these days! What does your daily schedule look like?"

You: "Thanks! Yeah, I follow a pretty strict routine. I usually wake up at 6:00 a.m., take a bath, and make sure I finish breakfast before 9:00 a.m."

Friend: "Nice! How much time do you dedicate to studying?"

You: "I break it down into sessions. First, I study for two hours, then I take a 20-minute break to stretch. After the break, I study for another two hours before having lunch at 1:00 p.m."

Friend: "Don't you get tired during the day?"

You: "I used to, but now after lunch, I sleep for two hours to recharge. At 4:00 p.m., I start another study block for a couple of hours."

Friend: "When do you get time for fitness or relaxation?"

You: "Around 5:00 p.m., I usually have a cup of tea to refresh my mind. After finishing my tea, I go straight to the gym. Then I eat dinner before 9:00 p.m. and head to bed at 11:00 p.m."

8. Quick Writing & Correction Labs

1. Fix the Error: "He go to gym at 6:00 p.m. after have tea."

Correction: "He goes to the gym at 6:00 p.m. after having tea."

2. Combine into One Long Sentence: "I eat dinner. The time is 8:30 p.m. After dinner I go to bed."

Example: "I eat dinner before 9:00 p.m., and after finishing my meal, I go to bed."

9. Moving Forward (70% Old + 30% New)

70% Old Review: Present simple routines, exact clock times with at, time duration with for, and sequential order using first, then, after.

30% New Concept: Deep usage of have / has / had, tiny words (before, after, to), and building long conversations using the "And-Because-So" chain.

10. Tonight's Homework Challenge (20 Minutes)

  1. Speaking (10 mins): Read the entire Long Conversation Role-Play (Section 7) out loud two times. Practice changing your tone naturally!
  2. Writing (5 mins): Write 3 sentences using "before," "after," and "for" about your actual day.
  3. Quiz (5 mins): Complete the interactive quiz below!

Quick Fluency Check

1. Which sentence correctly uses HAS/HAVE?

2. Fill in the blank: "I study _____ two hours every afternoon."

3. Choose the correct form: "After _____ my tea, I go to the gym."
